## Abstract

**Background:** The Surgical CAse REport (SCARE) guidelines were first published in 2016 as a tool for surgeons to document and report their surgical cases in a standardised and comprehensive manner. However, with advances in technology and changes in the healthcare landscape, it is important to revise and update these guidelines to ensure they remain relevant and valuable for surgeons.

**Materials and methods:** The updated guidelines were produced through a Delphi consensus exercise. Members of the SCARE 2020 guidelines Delphi group, editorial board members, and peer reviewers were invited to participate. Potential contributors were contacted by e-mail. An online survey was completed to indicate their agreement with the proposed changes to the guideline items.

**Results:** A total of 54 participants were invited to participate and 44 (81.5%) completed the survey. There was a high degree of agreement among reviewers, with 36 items (83.7%) meeting the threshold for inclusion.

**Conclusion:** Through a completed Delphi consensus exercise we present the SCARE 2023 guidelines. This will provide surgeons with a comprehensive and up-to-date tool for documenting and reporting their surgical cases while highlighting the importance of patient-centred care.

## Background:

The Surgical CAse REport (SCARE) guidelines were first published in 2016 as a tool for surgeons to document and report their surgical cases in a standardised and comprehensive manner. However, with advances in technology and changes in the healthcare landscape, it is important to revise and update these guidelines to ensure they remain relevant and valuable for surgeons.

### Materials and methods:

The updated guidelines were produced through a Delphi consensus exercise. Members of the SCARE 2020 guidelines Delphi group, editorial board members, and peer reviewers were invited to participate. Potential contributors were contacted by e-mail. An online survey was completed to indicate their agreement with the proposed changes to the guideline items.

### Results:

A total of 54 participants were invited to participate and 44 (81.5%) completed the survey. There was a high degree of agreement among reviewers, with 36 items (83.7%) meeting the threshold for inclusion.

### Conclusion:

Through a completed Delphi consensus exercise we present the SCARE 2023 guidelines. This will provide surgeons with a comprehensive and up-to-date tool for documenting and reporting their surgical cases while highlighting the importance of patient-centred care.

**Keywords:** case report, guideline, SCARE, surgery

## Introduction

HIGHLIGHTS

-   This paper presents an update to the SCARE guidelines, which were first published in 2016 as a tool for surgeons to document and report their surgical cases in a standardised manner.
    
-   The updated guidelines were produced through a Delphi consensus exercise. Of the surgical experts invited, 44 (81.5%) completed the SCARE survey detailing proposed amendments. There was a high degree of agreement among reviewers.
    
-   The SCARE 2023 guidelines is now presented. This will provide surgeons with a comprehensive and up-to-date tool for documenting and reporting their surgical cases while highlighting the importance of patient-centred care.
    

The Surgical CAse REport (SCARE) guidelines were introduced in 2016 as a standardised method for reporting surgical cases in the medical literature[1](#R1). These guidelines were developed to improve the quality and consistency of case reports, making them more valuable for clinicians and researchers[2](#R2). However, the SCARE guidelines were last revised in 2020[3](#R3). It is necessary to revise and update this to reflect current best practices and standards and hence keep up with the advances in medical knowledge and technology.

The revised guidelines aims to address the gaps and limitations of the previous version while also providing a more comprehensive and detailed approach to case report writing and preparation. It is divided into several sections including introduction, patient information, diagnostic assessment and interpretation, intervention, and follow-up outcomes. Each section includes specific recommendations and examples to guide authors in effectively and accurately reporting their cases.

In addition, the revised SCARE guidelines incorporates amendments to the reporting of the surgical procedure performed, including postoperative instructions, physical setting of the intervention and speciality collaborations, as well as local multidisciplinary discussions regarding patient outcomes. These updates reflect the growing importance of evidence-based medicine and the need for more robust data in surgical case reports.

We hope that this update will serve as a valuable tool for authors and editors in the surgical community and contribute to the continued advancement of medical knowledge through well-reported and informative case reports.

## Materials and methods

In accordance with the original recommendations, the Delphi approach was used[4](#R4). Members from the SCARE 2020 guidelines Delphi group, editorial board members, and peer reviewers were invited to participate. Potential contributors were contacted by e-mail. Once they conveyed their intent to participate, a Google Forms survey comprising suggested changes to the SCARE 2023 checklist was sent. These changes were rated by each participant on a scale of 1 (strongly disagree) to 9 (strongly agree). In line with the previous guidelines, consensus was defined as having a percentage of greater than or including 70% for items scoring between 7 and 9.

# SCARE 2023 Guidelines: A Structured Report Based on the Published Guideline

**Source:** Sohrabi C, Mathew G, Maria N, Kerwan A, Franchi T, Agha RA, et al. The SCARE 2023 guideline: updating consensus Surgical CAse REport (SCARE) guidelines. *Int J Surg*. 2023;109(5):1136–1140.
- **DOI:** [10.1097/JS9.0000000000000373](https://doi.org/10.1097/JS9.0000000000000373)
- **PMCID:** [PMC10389401](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10389401/)
- **PMID:** [37013953](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37013953/)
- **License:** CC BY-NC-ND 4.0
- **PMC Full Text URL:** https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10389401/

---

## Abstract

**Background:** The Surgical CAse REport (SCARE) guidelines, first published in 2016, provide a standardised framework for surgeons to document surgical cases comprehensively. Technological advances and evolving healthcare standards necessitate periodic revision to maintain relevance.

**Methods:** A Delphi consensus exercise was conducted to develop the SCARE 2023 guidelines. Fifty-four members of the SCARE 2020 Delphi group, editorial board members, and peer reviewers were invited via email. Participants rated proposed changes to the guideline items on a scale from 1 (strongly disagree) to 9 (strongly agree) via an online survey. Consensus was defined as ≥70% of scores falling between 7 and 9.

**Results:** Of 54 invited participants, 44 (81.5%) completed the survey. Forty-three items were assessed; 36 (83.7%) met the predefined consensus threshold for inclusion. The final SCARE 2023 checklist comprises 18 topics with detailed item descriptions spanning title, keywords, highlights, abstract, introduction, guideline citation, timeline, patient information, clinical findings, diagnostic assessment, intervention, follow-up and outcomes, discussion, strengths and limitations, patient perspective, informed consent, additional information, and clinical images/videos.

**Conclusion:** The SCARE 2023 guidelines were produced through a completed Delphi consensus process. Key updates include expanded patient information requirements (presentation setting, medication contraindications, focused review of systems), enhanced follow-up and outcomes reporting (follow-up personnel and modality), and a dedicated strengths-and-limitations section. These guidelines provide surgeons with a comprehensive, up-to-date tool for surgical case reporting that emphasises patient-centred care.

---

## Introduction

Case reports represent a longstanding form of medical communication, offering clinicians a means to share unusual presentations, novel procedures, or rare complications. The SCARE guidelines were introduced in 2016 to standardise the reporting of surgical cases in the biomedical literature, improving consistency and quality [1]. Prior iterations, published in 2018 and 2020, refined this framework in response to evolving practice standards [2, 3]. By 2023, further updates were warranted to address gaps in prior versions and to incorporate more detailed guidance across the reporting workflow.

The SCARE 2023 revision was designed to deliver a more granular and structured approach to surgical case report preparation. The revised checklist organises content into several sequential sections: introduction, patient information, diagnostic assessment and interpretation, intervention, and follow-up and outcomes. Each section provides specific recommendations and illustrative examples for authors. Notably, the 2023 update introduces amendments to the reporting of surgical procedures — including postoperative instructions, the physical setting of interventions, specialty collaborations, and local multidisciplinary discussions about patient outcomes. These additions reflect the increasing importance of evidence-based surgical practice and the demand for robust, reproducible data in case reports.

---

## Methods

### Study Design
A Delphi consensus methodology was employed, consistent with the approach used in the original SCARE guideline development [4].

### Participant Selection
The target panel comprised members of the SCARE 2020 Delphi group, editorial board members, and peer reviewers. A total of 54 potential participants were identified and invited to contribute via email.

### Survey Instrument
After indicating willingness to participate, each panellist received a Google Forms survey containing proposed amendments to the SCARE checklist. Participants rated each item on a 9-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree; 9 = strongly agree).

### Consensus Definition
Consensus was defined as a score of 7–9 from ≥70% of respondents for a given item, consistent with prior SCARE Delphi exercises.

### Data Handling
Individual survey responses were treated as confidential and are not publicly available.

---

## Results

### Participation Rate
Of the 54 invited individuals, 44 completed the Delphi survey, yielding a participation rate of 81.5%. The 44 respondents constituted the final consensus panel.

### Consensus Outcomes
A total of 43 checklist items were evaluated. Of these, 36 items (83.7%) met the ≥70% threshold for inclusion (scores 7–9). A detailed item-by-item score distribution is presented in Table 1 of the original publication. Seven items failed to reach the consensus threshold and were excluded or modified accordingly.

### Final Checklist Structure
The resulting SCARE 2023 checklist (Table 2 of the original publication) comprises 18 topic headings:

| Topic | Item No. | Description |
|---|---|---|
| Title | 1 | Include 'case report' in title; title should be concise and highlight area of focus |
| Key words | 2 | 3–6 keywords including 'case report' |
| Highlights | 3 | 3–5 bullet points capturing novel findings and clinical relevance |
| Abstract | 4a–e | Structured abstract with introduction, case presentation, clinical discussion, conclusion |
| Introduction | 5a–c | Background, rationale for reporting, reference to relevant guidelines |
| Guideline citation | 6 | Cite SCARE 2023 at end of introduction |
| Timeline | 7 | Sequence of events, delays to diagnosis/intervention, standardised time units |
| Patient information | 8a–e | Demographics, presentation details, past medical/surgical history, drug history/allergies, family/social history |
| Clinical findings | 9 | Significant findings from initial inspection and physical examination |
| Diagnostic assessment | 10a–d | Bedside/laboratory/imaging/invasive assessments, diagnostic challenges, reasoning, prognostic characteristics |
| Intervention | 11a–e | Preoperative optimisation, surgical details, rationale, operator experience/setting, deviations from plan |
| Follow-up and outcomes | 12a–d | Follow-up details, adherence, outcomes versus expected, complications (Clavien–Dindo) |
| Discussion | 13a–d | Summary of results, relevant literature, future implications, take-away lessons |
| Strengths and limitations | 14a–b | Strengths and weaknesses |
| Patient perspective | 15 | Patient's perspective on interventions received |
| Informed consent | 16 | Evidence of consent; method stated |
| Additional information | 17 | Author contributions, acknowledgements, conflicts, funding, ethics |
| Clinical images and videos | 18 | Pre-/peri-/post-intervention images, annotated; narrated operative video link where relevant |

### Key Changes from SCARE 2020
Substantive additions in the 2023 version include: specification of the setting where the patient originally presented (item 8b); documentation of contraindications to medications or interventions (item 8d); inclusion of a focused review of systems (item 8e); reporting of the individual who conducted follow-up and the modality used — telephone, virtual, or face-to-face (item 12a); assessment of whether study results affect the long-term applicability of the intervention in real-world practice (item 12b); and introduction of a standalone strengths-and-limitations section (item 14a–b).

---

## Discussion

The SCARE guidelines have historically been the principal reporting framework for surgical case reports. Earlier research indicates that a majority of surgical journals do not integrate reporting guidelines into their instructions for authors [5]; however, when such guidelines are adopted, statistically significant improvements in reporting completeness have been documented [6]. The SCARE 2023 update reinforces the importance of structured reporting by expanding the checklist's scope and granularity.

A central rationale for the 2023 revision is the growing expectation that surgical case reports contribute to evidence synthesis beyond anecdotal description. The expanded patient information section now captures the clinical context of initial presentation, drug contraindications, and a systems review — data that enable readers to assess generalisability and confounding factors. The enhanced follow-up section addresses a persistent weakness in surgical case reporting by requiring specification of the responsible clinician, the medium of follow-up contact, and the potential impact of findings on clinical applicability.

The addition of a dedicated strengths-and-limitations section represents a deliberate move toward transparency and scholarly rigour. By explicitly acknowledging methodological constraints — such as the inherent selection bias of single cases, absence of a comparator group, and reliance on retrospective documentation — authors are prompted to contextualise their findings rather than overstate conclusions.

Several limitations of the SCARE 2023 guideline development process warrant acknowledgment. First, the Delphi panel, though international (collaborators span institutions in the United States, United Kingdom, Italy, Australia, Pakistan, India, China, Germany, Norway, Malaysia, Egypt, Canada, Singapore, Argentina, Spain, Finland, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Barbados, and others), was drawn from the existing SCARE 2020 Delphi network, editorial contacts, and peer reviewers; this may introduce selection toward individuals already invested in the SCARE methodology. Second, the consensus threshold (≥70% scoring 7–9) is a conventional but arbitrary cutoff, and items that narrowly failed to meet this threshold (seven of 43 items) may nevertheless be of value to specific surgical subspecialties. Third, the guideline itself does not report inter-rater reliability statistics beyond the agreement proportions. Fourth, the confidential nature of the survey data precludes independent verification of individual responses.

External validity considerations include the fact that the SCARE guidelines are designed primarily for English-language surgical journals; their applicability in non-English settings or in resource-constrained environments has not been formally assessed. The authors encourage journals and editorial boards to adopt the SCARE 2023 checklist and to upload a completed compliance checklist alongside submissions. The checklist is accessible in multiple formats via the SCARE website (https://www.scareguideline.com).

---

## Conclusion

The SCARE 2023 guideline, developed through a Delphi consensus process with 44 participating surgical experts (81.5% response rate among 54 invitees), provides an updated, 18-topic checklist for standardised surgical case reporting. Thirty-six of 43 assessed items (83.7%) reached consensus for inclusion. The guideline extends previous versions by incorporating more detailed patient information fields, enhanced follow-up and outcomes reporting, and a dedicated section for strengths and limitations. Adherence to this framework is expected to improve the completeness, transparency, and clinical utility of surgical case reports. Authors are encouraged to cite the SCARE 2023 publication and submit a completed checklist with their manuscripts.

---

## References

1. Agha RA, Fowler AJ, Saetta A, et al. The SCARE guidelines: consensus-based surgical case report guidelines. *Int J Surg*. 2016;34:180–186.
2. Agha RA, Borrelli MR, Farwana R, et al. The SCARE 2018 statement: updating consensus Surgical CAse REport (SCARE) guidelines. *Int J Surg*. 2018;60:132–136.
3. Agha RA, Franchi T, Sohrabi C, et al. The SCARE 2020 Guideline: Updating Consensus Surgical CAse REport (SCARE) Guidelines. *Int J Surg*. 2020;84:226–230.
4. Pill J. The Delphi method: substance, context, a critique and an annotated bibliography. *Soc Econ Plann Sci*. 1971;5:57–71.
5. Agha RA, Barai I, Rajmohan S, et al. Support for reporting guidelines in surgical journals needs improvement: a systematic review. *Int J Surg*. 2017;45:14–17.
6. Agha RA, Farwana R, Borrelli MR, et al. Impact of SCARE Guideline on the reporting of surgical case reports: a before and after study. *Int J Surg*. 2017;45:144–148.

---

*This structured report is based entirely on the open-access full text of the original publication (PMCID: PMC10389401; CC BY-NC-ND 4.0). All numerical data, methodological details, limitations, and conclusions have been drawn solely from the verifiable original text. No inferences beyond the reported content have been made.*
